texts.text: The Fingerprint in the Blood
In November 1983 a 15-year-old girl was murdered in the Leicestershire village of Narborough, and the homicide went unsolved.

texts.text: In the summer of 1986 a second 15-year-old was slain near neighbouring Enderby.
A 17-year-old local youth confessed to the second killing, and to detectives the perplexing investigation was seemingly resolved.
The revelation had come two years previously.
On 10 September 1984 Alec Jeffreys, a geneticist at the University of Leicester, discerned on an X-ray film molecular markers whose layout varied considerably from person to person.
He called them DNA fingerprints, since, like fingerprints, they differentiated individuals.
The journal Nature promptly carried his paper in March 1985.
Police enlisted Jeffreys, and his genetic tests overturned the erroneous confession.
The youth was not the perpetrator, and the same attacker had killed both girls.
The youth became the first person known to be cleared by DNA evidence.
The forensic innovation had freed an innocent before it implicated anyone.
In January 1987 police commenced the world's first large-scale DNA screening, asking more than 5,000 men in three villages for blood or saliva.

texts.text: None matched.
The elusive killer, a local baker, had induced a co-worker to give a sample in his name, evading suspicion.
In August 1987 someone overheard the co-worker discussing the substitution and notified police.
Colin Pitchfork was detained on 19 September 1987, and his DNA profile matched.
In January 1988 he pleaded guilty and was jailed for life, the first person convicted of murder on the basis of DNA evidence.

texts.text: A tip-off, not the screening, had unmasked him.
The test's first beneficiary had been a blameless juvenile who had falsely admitted the offence.
